Weekly Calcifediol 100 µg in Women with Vitamin D Deficiency: A Post Hoc Analysis of a Randomised Placebo-Controlled Phase II/III Trial.
Background/Objective: Given the high prevalence of vitamin D deficiency, particularly among older women, this post hoc analysis was conducted to evaluate the long-term efficacy and safety of weekly calcifediol 100 µg in women with vitamin D deficiency participating in a randomised, double-blind, phase II/III trial. Methods: A total of 261 women were included (calcifediol, n = 192; placebo, n = 69). The primary objective was to compare the proportions of women achieving serum 25(OH)D concentrations ≥20 ng/mL or ≥30 ng/mL over the 12-month treatment period. Exploratory analyses of body mass index (BMI) and menopausal status were performed. Results: Weekly calcifediol 100 µg demonstrated superior efficacy versus placebo from week 4 in women achieving ≥20 ng/mL (68.2% vs. 5.8%; p < 0.001) or ≥30 ng/mL (21.4% vs. 0%; p < 0.001), and consistently higher proportions were maintained through week 52. Mean 25(OH)D concentrations increased from 12.21 ng/mL at baseline to 39.47 ng/mL at week 16, and remained stable (41-43 ng/mL) thereafter. No significant differences were observed across BMI or menopausal status subgroups. The safety profile of weekly calcifediol 100 µg was similar to placebo, with no evidence of toxicity. Conclusions: Weekly calcifediol 100 µg is a safe and effective option for achieving and maintaining adequate vitamin D levels in vitamin D-deficient women over a period of 12 months, and is associated with consistent effects across BMI and menopausal status.

SOURCE EXCERPT (PubMed 43021726):
Oral versus intravenous postoperative antibiotics after laparoscopic appendectomy following complicated appendicitis: an open-label cluster-randomized cluster-crossover multiperiod non-inferiority study.
The optimal administration route and duration of postoperative antibiotics for complicated appendicitis after source control remain debated. The aim of this non-inferiority cluster-randomized trial was to compare oral versus intravenous antibiotics following laparoscopic appendectomy. In this pragmatic, open-label, cluster-randomized, cluster-crossover, non-inferiority trial across 12 Danish hospitals, adults undergoing laparoscopic appendectomy for complicated appendicitis received either a 3-day oral or intravenous postoperative antibiotic regimen. The primary outcome was 30-day intra-abdominal abscess, analysed in both intention-to-treat and per-protocol populations using a 5% points non-inferiority margin. Secondary 30-day outcomes included length of hospital stay, readmission, and postoperative complications. Of 5424 patients screened, 1021 with complicated appendicitis were allocated to oral (n = 567) or intravenous (n = 454) antibiotics. In the intention-to-treat analysis, intra-abdominal abscess occurred in 39 of 567 oral and 22 of 454 intravenous patients; weighted 30-day incidences were 6.8% and 4.9% (absolute risk difference, 1.9%; 90% c.i., -0.4 to 4.2), meeting non-inferiority. In the per-protocol analysis, abscess occurred in 19 of 395 and 9 of 294 patients; weighted incidences were 4.9% and 3.0% (absolute risk difference, 1.8%; 90% c.i., -0.3 to 3.9). Oral antibiotics shortened hospital stay (-41.1 h; 95% c.i., -46.7 to -35.6) but increased readmission (difference, 4.7%; 95% c.i., 0.5 to 8.9). A 3-day oral antibiotic regimen was non-inferior to intravenous antibiotic therapy in preventing intra-abdominal abscess after laparoscopic appendectomy for complicated appendicitis. Reduced hospital stay and comparable clinical outcomes support oral antibiotics as a routine postoperative option in clinically stable patients. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04803422.

SOURCE EXCERPT (PubMed 43015686):
Efficacy and safety of urokinase intravenous thrombolysis in minor stroke according to large vessel occlusion status: a subgroup analysis of the TRUST trial.
The risk-benefit profile of thrombolytic therapy in minor stroke patients with large vessel occlusion (LVO) remains uncertain. This post hoc analysis of the TRUST trial (ThRombolysis with Urokinase for minor Stroke Trial) sought to comparatively assess whether the presence of large vessel occlusion (LVO) modifies the efficacy and safety of urokinase intravenous thrombolysis, compared with best medical treatment(BMT), in patients with minor stroke. This post-hoc exploratory analysis included patients from the TRUST trial with available vascular imaging data, categorized in the LVO and the non-LVO group. Each group was further divided into the UK thrombolysis group and the BMT group. Primary efficacy outcome was the proportion of patients achieving a modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 0-1 at 90 days. Safety outcomes included symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH) within 36 h and all-cause mortality within 90 days. Of the 999 patients enrolled in the TRUST trial, 605 were included in the current study. UK thrombolysis was not associated with a 90-day excellent functional outcome in minor stroke patients, either in LVO patients (adjusted risk ratio [RR] 1.90, 95% CI 0.63-2.26) or in non-LVO patients (adjusted RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.84-1.23) compared with the BMT group (p for interaction = 0.41). In the LVO group, UK thrombolysis showed a non-significant trend toward reduced mortality (adjusted RR 0.04, 95% CI 0.01-1.65), whereas no such effect was observed in non-LVO patients (adjusted RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.11-2.52). No significant interaction was found between groups (p for interaction = 0.25). In addition, there were no patients who experienced sICH in subgroup analysis. Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) remains a key challenge for patients receiving moderately emetogenic chemotherapy (MEC), especially those at high risk. The DAPA-TAVI trial demonstrated that dapagliflozin reduced the composite of all-cause mortality or worsening heart failure (HF) at 1 year in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with prior HF. Whether the magnitude of this benefit differs according to diabetes mellitus (DM) status remains uncertain. This pre-specified subgroup analysis of the multicenter randomized DAPA-TAVI trial conducted at 39 centers in Spain, which enrolled 1222 patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing TAVR with prior HF and at least one high-risk condition. Patients were stratified by the presence or absence of DM. The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality or worsening HF at 12 months. Secondary endpoints included the individual components of the primary endpoint, cardiovascular death, and safety outcomes. Cox proportional-hazards models adjusted for age, sex, coronary artery disease, baseline ejection fraction and baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate were used to estimate treatment effects. Among 1222 patients, 537 (43.9%) had DM. In patients with DM, dapagliflozin significantly reduced the primary endpoint compared with standard care (15.2% vs. 22.7%; HR 0.580; 95% CI 0.389-0.866; p = 0.008; number needed to treat [NNT] = 11), driven primarily by fewer worsening HF events. In patients without DM, the reduction was numerically lower and non-significant (15.0% vs. 18.0%; HR 0.814; 95% CI 0.560-1.183; p = 0.280; NNT = 32). Genital infections were more frequent with dapagliflozin in patients with DM, whereas symptomatic hypotension was more common in those without DM. No significant differences in serious adverse events were observed in either subgroup. No statistically significant interactions between DM status and treatment effect were observed for the primary or secondary endpoints. In this pre-specified subanalysis of the DAPA-TAVI trial, dapagliflozin significantly reduced the risk of death or worsening HF in patients with DM undergoing TAVR, with a favorable benefit-risk profile, whereas a more modest and non-significant effect was observed in non-DM patients. Although no statistically significant interaction according to diabetes status was observed, the apparently greater benefit among patients with DM warrants further investigation.

SOURCE EXCERPT (PubMed 42983692):
Efficacy of chlorhexidine vaginal preparation in reducing postoperative infections during emergency cesarean deliveries for women in labor: a randomized controlled trial.
Postoperative infections are a leading cause of maternal morbidity after emergency cesarean delivery. This trial explores the effectiveness of preoperative vaginal cleansing via the use of chlorhexidine for reducing these complications in women in labor. This single-blinded superiority randomized controlled trial included 840 women in labor equally distributed to either immediate preoperative chlorhexidine gluconate 0.05% vaginal cleansing or no-cleansing; 826 were analyzed under a modified intention-to-treat approach. The co-primary outcomes were postcesarean endometritis and surgical site infection (SSI). Secondary outcomes included composite wound complications, postoperative fever, significant leukocytosis, hospital readmission, length of stay, and adverse drug reactions. Effects are expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals, with adjusted, sensitivity, and subgroup analyses for the co-primary outcomes. Chlorhexidine significantly reduced both co-primary outcomes; postcesarean endometritis (1.9% vs. 6.3%; RR 0.303, 95% CI 0.139-0.662; P = 0.001) and SSI (1.4% vs. 5.4%; RR 0.269, 95% CI 0.110-0.656; P = 0.002); both remained significant against a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.025. Other outcomes were also reduced, including composite wound complications (3.4% vs. 11.0%; RR 0.307, 95% CI 0.171-0.550; P < 0.001), and readmission for infection (1.4% vs. 6.3%; P < 0.001; RR 0.227, 95% CI 0.095-0.547). The co-primary outcome effects persisted after adjustment and in sensitivity analyses. Treatment effects were in the same direction across premature rupture of membranes (PROM) and obesity subgroups with no significant interaction, although the SSI reduction reached significance overall and in the non-obese stratum but not within the obese stratum. As a low-cost intervention that can be integrated into existing perioperative workflows, it is a promising strategy for reducing maternal infection; however, adverse events were not systematically solicited, and neonatal exposure was not assessed. Limosilactobacillus reuteri for oral mucositis in patients undergoing radiotherapy for malignant head and neck tumors: a randomized controlled trial.
Oral mucositis (OM) is a major toxicity in patients with head and neck cancer undergoing radiotherapy. Here we conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized phase II trial (NCT06285591) from March 2024 to January 2025 at West China Hospital of Sichuan University to evaluate whether Limosilactobacillus reuteri (L. reuteri) supplementation could reduce severe OM (SOM; WHO Oral Toxicity criteria grade ≥3). A total of 160 patients were randomly assigned to receive L. reuteri probiotic lozenges or placebo twice daily during radiotherapy. The primary endpoint was the incidence of SOM, and secondary endpoints included SOM onset and duration, as well as the incidence, onset, and duration of any-grade OM. Safety outcomes were monitored throughout the study. The primary endpoint was met, with a lower incidence of SOM in the L. reuteri group than in the placebo group (37.5% vs 61.3%; relative risk 0.61; 95% confidence interval 0.44-0.85; absolute risk reduction 23.8 percentage points, 95% CI 8.7% to 38.8%; P = 0.004). L. reuteri supplementation also delayed SOM onset and shortened SOM duration. No significant safety concerns were observed. These findings indicate that L. reuteri supplementation reduces SOM incidence and severity in patients with head and neck cancer receiving radiotherapy.
